title: Malbim on Nahum
text: The burden of Nineveh. This book is divided into two parts. One is called “The Burden of Nineveh,” comprising the prophecies in chapters 1 and 2; the second is the Book of the Vision of Nahum, comprising the prophecy in chapter 3. For Nineveh was destroyed twice. The burden relates the first destruction of Nineveh, which occurred either before the prophet’s time or during his lifetime, while the vision concerns distant times, in which he foresaw Nineveh’s second destruction. This took place in the first year of Nebuchadnezzar’s reign, when the city was utterly destroyed. Now, the second destruction of Nineveh, which was brought about by Nebuchadnezzar, is mentioned in the words of our Sages. The first destruction, however, is not found in the works of our Sages, but is an accepted account related in all the ancient chronicles. This is their account: Sardanapalus, king of Assyria, was a wicked man—a glutton, a drunkard, a pursuer of immorality, foolish, and exceedingly corrupt. The commander of the Babylonian army, whose name was Belesys and who was under his rule, conspired against him together with the commander of the Median army, whose name was Arbaces, and the other military commanders. They assembled with their forces, numbering about four hundred thousand men, to wage war against Nineveh. The king went out against them, struck down many of them, and pursued them as far as the border of the land of the Chaldeans, where the rebels made their stand. They then learned that a great army had come out of Bactria to aid the king, so they sent messengers to meet them and persuade them to join the conspiracy. The king knew nothing of this and placed his trust in the mighty men who had come to assist him. They ate, drank, and became intoxicated; then the conspirators rose against them at night and struck down the king’s entire army. The king’s forces that went out against them, together with their commander Shalman, the brother of the king’s wife, also fell in battle. All the commanders who had been subordinate to him rebelled and cast off his yoke. The king and his remaining forces then shut themselves within the city of Nineveh, which was a fortified city surrounded by the Tigris River. The rebels besieged the city for three years but could not capture it. The sorcerers told the king that so long as the Tigris River did not turn against him as an enemy, the city would not be taken. He trusted in this and feared no harm. After three years, however, the river overflowed its banks and breached the city wall for a distance of about half a parasang. When the king saw that the river had turned against him as an enemy, he was greatly terrified and despaired. He ordered a great pyre of wood and fire to be erected in his palace, placed all his possessions upon it, and then he himself, together with the queen and his concubines, ascended the pyre, and they were all consumed by fire. The enemies conquered the city but did not lay their hands upon its spoils. Nor did they wish to harm its inhabitants, for they said that they had come only to destroy the royal house. Nevertheless, fear fell upon the people of the city, and they all fled, leaving the city as desolate as a wilderness. The enemy erected a monument of contempt and disgrace to King Sardanapalus as a memorial to his evil deeds, while all the monuments of honor that had testified to the king’s glory they shattered and demolished, making him a sign and a byword. This is the substance of the account found unanimously in all the chronicles. But when did this event occur, and at what time? We cannot extract from their words anything certain or clear. The commentators say that King Sardanapalus was Esarhaddon, who is mentioned in Scripture and who reigned after Sennacherib, whose sons struck him down with the sword. They say that “Sardanapalus” is a compound name: Sar means Assur, while napal refers to Haddon and Pul, who are mentioned in Chronicles. According to this, the event occurred at the end of Hezekiah’s reign or during the reign of Manasseh, and this accords with the opinion of our Sages that Nahum prophesied in the days of Manasseh. Yet one who examines the historical chronicles will understand that it occurred much earlier. We have no means of deciding the matter. If it occurred earlier, Nahum delivered the burden concerning a destruction that had taken place before his time; and if it occurred in his lifetime, he delivered the burden concerning a destruction that took place in his own time. Concerning this he said, “The burden of Nineveh.” In addition, he beheld a vision concerning Nineveh’s second destruction, which would occur in the days of Nebuchadnezzar. Concerning this he said, “The book of the vision,” for a vision concerns the future. We shall explain the verses in a manner consistent with all these possibilities.

God, he first presents an introduction and preface to his book: “Hashem is a jealous and avenging God.” That is, He possesses two attributes: first, to be jealous for the honor of His desecrated Name; and second, to avenge the evil committed in opposition to Him. There is a distinction between them. When He avenges the evil that the wicked have actually committed, He does not remain slow to anger; rather, “Hashem avenges”—He takes vengeance immediately, so that they will not persist in their wickedness and destroy the world. But when He is jealous for the honor of His Name, He does not take vengeance immediately; rather, He is “a Master of wrath.” The defining feature of wrath is that one preserves his anger within his heart and does not bring it into action by imposing punishment, for anger expressed through punishment is called “anger.” The prophet now explains these two matters: “He takes vengeance upon His adversaries, and He reserves wrath for His enemies.” There is a distinction between an adversary and an enemy. An adversary is one who actively causes distress, whereas an enemy is one who desires another’s harm in his heart but does not actively cause him distress. It is possible for someone to be an adversary without being an enemy, when he causes harm for his own benefit rather than out of hatred; and one may be an enemy without being an adversary, when he does not actually inflict harm. In relation to God, those who actively commit evils against their fellow human beings are called Hashem’s adversaries, even though such a person may not be His enemy, since he may act merely for his own benefit. Those who willfully deny Him and oppose belief in Hashem are called His enemies, even though they may not actively harm their fellow human beings. There is also a distinction between vengeance and bearing a grudge: bearing a grudge means preserving hatred within the heart, whereas vengeance means taking action to punish. Therefore, Scripture says that against “His adversaries,” who actively commit evil, Hashem “takes vengeance” immediately and does not wait; but toward “His enemies,” who deny His Divinity without actively inflicting harm, He “reserves” the wrath within His heart and does not punish them immediately.

“Hashem is slow to anger.” He explains the meaning of reserving wrath: in this respect, He is slow to anger and does not punish immediately. This is because He is “great in power,” as it is written, “And now, I pray, let the power of Hashem be great, as You have spoken, saying: ‘Hashem is slow to anger.’” Slowness to anger demonstrates the greatness of His power, for He is able to endure the present offense and punish whenever He chooses. A human being cannot remain slow to anger because his power to endure is limited. He also fears that by tomorrow he may no longer possess the power to punish, since his strength does not endure. But Hashem, because He is great in power, is slow to anger. Nevertheless, “He will by no means acquit,” for in the end He will punish and destroy His enemies when the measure of their sin is full. By this, Nahum means that Hashem granted Nineveh an extension from the time Jonah prophesied against it. Although at that time its people repented only of the violence in their hands and did not repent of worshipping other gods, as explained there, God waits until the measure of sin is full before punishing idolatry, heresy, and denial of faith; their punishment had not yet reached its completion. It was only because of their violence—on account of which they are called “adversaries”—that He sought to destroy them immediately, within forty days. The prophet therefore first presented Hashem’s attribute and His manner of governing the punishment of the wicked, explaining how He remained slow to anger toward them until their end arrived. He now begins to describe the nature of His punishment and vengeance. He portrays Hashem’s coming and revelation to destroy the wicked in three successive stages, depicting each stage through a different image that is exceedingly awesome, tumultuous, and terrifying. He clothes his poetic expression in frightening visions, as though the four mighty foundations of the earth—the four elements—were going forth with Him to devastate and destroy the entire face of the earth. In the first stage, he depicts Hashem stirring Himself to descend from the highest heavens to the earth in order to destroy it. He portrays the progress of the Divine King in holiness accompanied by the two elements through which poets represent His path and movement: the element of air and the element of water. Therefore, he says, “Hashem—His way is in the whirlwind and in the storm.” The path by which He travels toward the earth is through the whirlwind and storm, and He rides upon a swift cloud bearing the element of water. The “cloud” is “the dust of His feet,” as though, in the swiftness of His movement, He raises dust, which is the cloud. That is, the two elements that sometimes devastate inhabited lands will then be aroused: a raging storm that uproots mountains and shatters rocks, and torrents from the clouds, with floods and deluges of water.

“He rebukes.” The prophet depicts how He will then bring destruction both upon the sea and upon the dry land: “He rebukes the sea and dries it up, and He makes all the rivers desolate.” Although at a time of flooding, when the clouds burst open, the rivers fill with water and pour into the sea, He will bring about two contrary effects at once. Although the torrent of the sea will have passed over and inundated the land, the rivers will become dry and their waters will no longer flow into the sea, so that the sea itself will dry up. He will likewise bring destruction upon the dry land, for then “Bashan and Carmel will wither.” Through the storm, the torrent of hail, and the devastating tempest, all the grainfields will be cut down and the blossoms of the trees destroyed, as it is written: “The voice of Hashem is upon the waters; the voice of Hashem breaks the cedars,” and so forth.

“The mountains”—this is the second stage. When He reaches the summits of the lofty mountains along His path, He is then close to the earth. Here the prophet depicts the third destructive force going forth to perform its work: the element of earth. When He stands upon the mountaintops, “the mountains quake before Him,” and even “the hills,” which are lower than the mountains, “melt away.” That is, the element of earth will then be shaken, producing an earthquake. It will begin in the mountains, where earthquakes most commonly occur, and afterward spread to the hills. He adds that “the earth rises before Him,” as though the entire earth were lifting itself from its place to stand before Him, like one who rises before a great king. Together with it, “the world and all who dwell in it” will rise. This poetically signifies that the entire earth will then quake and its pillars will tremble. It is an image of universal destruction brought about through the shaking of the element of earth.

“Before.” This is the third stage, in which the Judge has already come to the earth, judged its inhabitants according to their deeds, and poured out indignation, fury, and distress upon them. Here the prophet depicts the fourth destructive force going forth to devastate and destroy: the element of fire. There is a distinction between anger, wrath, and fury. Wrath is the inward anger restrained within the heart. When that anger manifests itself outwardly, it is called anger, for punishment is then decreed. The curse and punishment themselves are called fury. Therefore, he says, “Who can stand before His fury?”—meaning the punishment itself. He adds, “Who can rise up even amid His fierce anger?” even before He has poured out His fury. He further adds that even His inward wrath, although it has not yet emerged outwardly, is nevertheless “poured out like fire.” He depicts this wrath as a burning fire confined within the eternal mountains and consuming down to the great abyss. When the fire is liquefied through sulfurous substances and other fiery materials found in the depths of the earth, and the earth spews forth the substances contained within it, His wrath is poured out like fire cast forth from mountains that discharge flames. Solid substances then melt, until even the mighty rocks “are shattered by Him,” rising like flying dust to devastate and destroy everything around them.

“Good.” After this terrifying depiction, in which the universal place—the globe of the earth—has descended into chaos and perished, leaving no place or foundation for anything existing upon the face of the earth, the prophet asks: Upon what will the inhabitants of the world now stand? Has not the earth crumbled and collapsed? He answers: “In the day of distress, Hashem is good as a stronghold.” It is good to rely upon Hashem, for He is now the Place of the world; upon Him the creatures will stand, and in Him they will find strength and refuge. “He knows those who take refuge in Him.” That is, the stronghold in which they will now seek shelter—Hashem—is superior to any stronghold that a person might find in something natural. A natural stronghold does not know who is sheltering within it, but Hashem is a stronghold who knows those who take refuge in Him and watches over each of them through individual Divine Providence. In other words, amid this universal destruction, He will watch with a compassionate eye to save those who trust in Him and rescue them from distress.

“With an overflowing flood.” Alongside the image of Hashem as a stronghold against distress, the prophet also depicts Him as passing through an overwhelming flood to eliminate the source of that distress. That is, when Hashem passes through with a flood and a torrent of water, “He will make a complete end of its place”—the place from which distress came upon the entire world, namely the land of Assyria. “And darkness will pursue His enemies.” This depicts the waters of the Tigris overflowing and inundating Nineveh at Hashem’s command. All the inhabitants of the city fled as though their path were dark and slippery and the angel of Hashem were pursuing them, as explained in verse 1.

“What do you devise concerning Hashem?” Why do you entertain an evil thought concerning Hashem, as though He had gone forth to do harm, to devour, and to destroy? Such conduct is not among His attributes. In truth, His intention is not to inflict evil; rather, “He is making a complete end; distress will not arise twice.” Through this He will eliminate the source of distress—namely, the kingdom of Assyria, which had been the scourge of the world. By means of this flood, He will eliminate the distress so that it will not arise twice. Although Assyria will arise once more after this downfall, it will eventually return to destruction a second time through Nebuchadnezzar; and after the second destruction, it will never arise again. Thus, distress will arise only once more, but not twice.

“For while they are entangled like thorns.” Through this flood, Sardanapalus became terrified and despaired. He arranged a mass of thorns to be kindled by fire, and he and his entire household ascended the pyre and were burned there. The prophet thus depicts the king and all the members of his household as drinking and becoming intoxicated, as was their custom, for they were continually among those who drank wine to excess. In their drunkenness, they came “among entangled thorns”—the mass of thorns and the fiery pyre. Although “the drunkards” were “in their drunken state,” meaning saturated with wine, nevertheless, when they approached the entangled thorns, “they were consumed like fully dried stubble.” That is, they were like stubble whose time of growth had been completed and which had dried out, so that it burns immediately upon encountering fire. Though they were moist with wine, they became like dry stubble.

“From you.” He turns to the city of Nineveh and addresses her: Behold, “from you has gone forth” this wicked man, “who devises evil against Hashem” by denying the existence of God and His Providence. He is “a counselor of wickedness,” advising others to cast off the Divine yoke and commit every abomination.

“Thus says Hashem.” Therefore, it was decreed that Nineveh would become desolate, and the fear of Hashem consequently came upon its inhabitants, causing them all to flee. “Though they were intact and likewise numerous,” meaning that they were a numerous people and their numbers had not been diminished in war, since they had not fought at all, nevertheless, “so were they shorn away” and fled from the city, “as he passed away”—the king who had devised evil against Hashem. According to those who say that the Sardanapalus involved in this event was Esarhaddon, son of Sennacherib, the prophet may be understood as addressing Sennacherib directly: “You who devise evil against Hashem! From you has gone forth a counselor of wickedness”—that is, Esarhaddon, who counseled wickedness by casting off the Divine yoke, came forth from you. You are Sennacherib, who devised evil against Hashem and sent messengers to blaspheme the living God. “Therefore, thus says Hashem: If they were shorn away intact and likewise numerous,” then “he too shall pass away.” That is, this counselor of wickedness will likewise pass away. For through this form of death—death by fire—many intact multitudes from Sennacherib’s camp were shorn away from the world: the angel who went forth and struck the Assyrian camp burned them all, according to the tradition of our Sages. Therefore, “he too shall pass away”—he too will pass through the fire. The verse uses the language of passing through fire because it was their practice to make their children pass through fire to Molech. Sennacherib himself wished to do this to his sons, which is why they struck him down with the sword, as explained in connection with the verse (Isaiah 30:33), “For Topheth has long been prepared; it too has been made ready for the king.” That is, this death—being burned upon the pyre—had been prepared for him since the days of his father. “And though I have afflicted you.” He now turns to Israel: The affliction that I brought upon you through Assyria—“I will afflict you no more.” This is especially fitting if we say that this event occurred during the reign of Esarhaddon, for Assyria then ceased afflicting Israel. If we say that it occurred earlier, Assyria nevertheless ceased afflicting them at that particular time, for the king had intended to wage war against Israel and oppress them, but the destruction of Nineveh frustrated his plan at that time.

“And now I will break his yoke.” This refers to the yoke of Assyria—the burden of taxation and servitude. “And I will tear your bonds apart”—the bonds by which you were restrained because of your fear of his troops and armies. If this event occurred during the reign of Manasseh, as explained above, then the yoke was broken completely, for from that time onward Assyria’s dominion over Israel ceased. If it occurred earlier, the meaning is that, at any rate, “now I will break it,” whereas Sennacherib’s later invasion of Israel still lay in the future.

“And Hashem has commanded concerning you.” He turns to Sardanapalus: Hashem has commanded and decreed concerning you that “your name shall be perpetuated no longer”—none of your descendants will arise as a king called by your name, for both he and his offspring have been wiped away, and his name will no longer be remembered. “From the house of your god I will cut off the carved image and the molten image.” It was customary for kings to erect statues in their own likenesses within the temples of their gods. The people honored the king’s image and attributed divinity to him. They then removed every statue that had served as a monument to his honor. In its place, they erected upon his grave a statue of disgrace, signifying his worthlessness and humiliation, as related in the historical chronicles. Therefore, He says: “I will make the carved and molten image your grave,” so that it will serve as a monument declaring that “you have become contemptible” and exceedingly despised.

“Behold, upon the mountains are the feet of one who brings good tidings.” This king sought to subjugate Judah, and its people were afraid of him, but news of his downfall came to them. According to the commentators who maintain that this event occurred in the days of Manasseh, Chronicles relates that the commanders of the king of Assyria captured Manasseh and brought him in chains to Babylon. Manasseh then entreated Hashem, who restored him to his kingdom. It is evident that he was captured by Belesys, the commander of the Babylonian army, who was then subordinate to the king of Assyria. Later, when the Babylonian commander rebelled against Sardanapalus, king of Assyria, he restored Manasseh to his kingdom. Chronicles further explains that Manasseh then made vows to serve Hashem. According to my interpretation, Psalm 66 was composed concerning this event, for it says, “I will fulfill to You my vows, which my lips uttered,” and so forth. Then messengers bearing good tidings went forth upon the mountains of Judah, proclaiming peace, for there was no longer any fear of the adversary. The prophet told them to “celebrate your festivals,” for the altar had been rebuilt and they had begun to worship Hashem, and to “fulfill your vows” that they had made in their time of distress. They need no longer fear the king of Assyria, whom the prophet previously called a counselor of wickedness, “for the wicked one shall no longer pass through you; he has been utterly cut off”—that is, both he and his household. Even according to my own view, that this event appears to have occurred earlier, the king intended to wage war against Judah and had already begun to harm the Ten Tribes. This was not mentioned in Scripture because his evil design was never carried out.

“He has come up.” “The one who scatters has already come up before you”—namely, the king of Assyria, who scattered Israel into exile, or intended to do so. Now, however, “he is confined within a fortress”: his own military commanders have besieged him, and he himself is under siege, as explained above (1:1). Therefore, “watch the road” for the arrival of good news concerning his downfall; “strengthen your loins and fortify your power exceedingly,” for you are about to hear good tidings.

“For Hashem has restored the pride of Jacob.” He also permitted the Ten Tribes, who had been exiled under his dominion, to return to their land, so that their glory would become like “the pride of Israel,” meaning the tribe of Judah, which had not been under his control. For until now, “plunderers had plundered them”: they resembled a vine whose fruit had been emptied out. Moreover, “they had destroyed their branches,” for they had ruined the branches of the vine itself. That is, besides plundering their possessions, they had exiled them from their land, leaving them unable to produce new branches or bear fruit. Even if we say that this event occurred in earlier times, we must conclude that the king of Assyria had already begun sending his armies against the Ten Tribes long before, although this is not mentioned in Scripture.

“The shield.” The prophet now returns to describe Nineveh’s first destruction in detail. At first, King Sardanapalus trusted in the multitude of his mighty warriors, who had prevailed in battle. “The shields of his mighty men” were “reddened,” dyed red as a sign that they would shed much blood and show no mercy. His “men of valor were clothed in scarlet”—they wore garments dyed with crimson as a symbol of bloodshed and murder. “The chariots were like fiery steel on the day they were prepared.” The chariots newly prepared for battle were treated with fiery steel—that is, with flames—so that they would appear new, as though they had been prepared that very day. “And the cypress spears were poisoned”—the spears made of cypress wood were smeared with poison and deadly venom.

“In the outer streets.” The outer streets are the areas behind the houses; there “the chariots rage wildly,” careening like madmen. “In the broad squares,” which are the open spaces before the houses, “they jostle together,” gathering in great numbers as people gather in a marketplace. Their appearance is like flaming torches, and they race with tremendous speed like flashes of lightning. Thus far, the prophet has described how the king prepared all his mighty warriors, chariots, and multitudes for battle.

“He remembers his nobles.” In addition, he recalls the mighty men—the army that came from Bactria to assist him, upon whom he relied to defeat the enemy. But “they stumbled as they advanced.” While traveling, they stumbled along the way; that is, a different spirit took hold of them, and they joined the rebels and turned against him. It was as though those who obstructed and enticed them away from going to his aid had caused them to stumble. Consequently, all the mighty warriors of his army faltered and fell in battle, as explained in the account that I cited at the beginning of the book. Then “they hastened to her wall”—they shut themselves within the city wall to seek protection from the adversary. “And the defensive covering was prepared”—they fortified the stronghold so that it would shelter them from the enemy.

“The gates of the rivers were opened.” Afterward, the Tigris River overflowed its bounds, its gates opened, and it inundated the city. Then “the palace melted away”—that is, the king and all the members of his royal household melted with fear, for his sorcerers had told him that when the river flooded the city, he would be delivered into the enemy’s hands.

“And Huzzab was uncovered and carried away.” A fiery pyre was then prepared to burn the queen and all the king’s concubines. “She was uncovered” refers to the queen, who was carried up to the pyre while covered within a canopied litter—the covered carriage in which nobles were borne. “Her maidservants” were likewise brought up to the fire. They moaned and lamented like the sound of doves, beating upon their hearts—striking their breasts in profound grief.

“And Nineveh was like a pool of water.” Through the Tigris River, which inundated it, Nineveh became like a pool filled with water. Yet “so it had been from ancient days”—had this not always been its condition, since the river had flooded it repeatedly from earliest times? Abravanel already wrote that Nineveh was always filled with water, so that its inhabitants had to build their homes upon elevated structures. Thus, this was a common occurrence there. Nevertheless, “they fled.” Fear came upon them because their diviners had given them a sign connected with the river’s flooding, and they all fled. “Stand! Stand!” We have already explained the account related in the ancient chronicles: the army that conquered Nineveh at that time assured the city’s inhabitants that they would do them no harm, for they had not come to wage war against the city but only to humble the pride of the wicked Sardanapalus. They therefore cried out to the inhabitants not to flee. This is the meaning of “Stand! Stand!”—thus they called to them, urging them not to flee. But “none turned back,” for trembling had seized them, and they fled though no one pursued them.

“Plunder!” It is further related in the historical chronicles that the victors did not wish to touch Nineveh’s spoils and did not lay their hands upon its plunder. The honor of victory and of having conquered the city was sufficient for them; they had not come for plunder or spoils. Accordingly, the prophet poetically addresses the victors: “Plunder the silver! Plunder the gold!” There is abundant spoil, for “there is no end to the treasure,” and the city contains limitless riches. The victors reply, “Honor is greater than every precious vessel.” That is, the honor of victory is more valuable and important to us than any precious object. We came for honor, not for spoil.

“Empty.” The prophet depicts the condition of the city’s inhabitants: everything has been emptied out—“emptiness and desolation”—and everything has been destroyed—“devastation.” The hearts of the city’s inhabitants melt from overwhelming fear; their knees tremble as they flee and escape; and anguish seizes every waist because of their crushing calamity and grief.

“Where is it?” The prophet now directs his attention toward the royal palace, which has been destroyed and left desolate. He marvels at the cruelty of Sardanapalus, who burned his wives and mercilessly killed his children. He asks, “Where is the lions’ den?” This is the royal palace, where the kings—the old lions—dwelt. “And the feeding place of the young lions,” for around the king’s palace the young lions grazed—that is, the king’s sons. “Where the lion and lioness walked,” for the lion and lioness—the king and queen—continually walked there. The “lion’s cub” also walked there, referring to the young royal children, “with none to frighten them,” for they lived there in complete security.

“The lion.” How, then, could such cruelty now have occurred there, that the lion tore apart his own cubs? That is, the king killed his young children. And “the lion strangled his lionesses,” for he ordered his wives—the lionesses—to be strangled, since they were suffocated by the smoke. “He filled his lairs with prey and his dens with torn flesh.” What he tore from among his wives is called terefah, “torn flesh,” in the feminine form, while what he tore from among his cubs is called teref, “prey,” in the masculine form. The prophet depicts the females as dwelling in dens and the cubs as inhabiting small lairs, in keeping with the metaphor of the lion. That is, the children were in small chambers, which he filled with their remains, while his wives were in his palaces, which he filled with their slain bodies. Has such a thing ever been heard of?

“Behold.” He answers: “Behold, I am against you, declares Hashem.” That is, all this occurred by Hashem’s decree. “I will burn her chariot in smoke”—the queen was brought up to the pyre together with her carriage and covered litter, as it is written, “Huzzab was uncovered and carried away,” and she was suffocated by the smoke of the pyre. “And the sword will devour your young lions”—the enemy’s sword will also devour his remaining sons. The commentators have already noted that lion hunters customarily fill the lion’s den with smoke, causing the young lions to emerge from their lairs, whereupon the hunters kill them with the sword. Through this, “I will cut off your prey from the earth,” so that you will no longer prey upon many nations. Furthermore, “the voice of your messengers shall no longer be heard”—the messengers through whom you blasphemed Hashem.

“Woe.” The prophet now begins the prophecy concerning the future, in which he foresaw Nineveh’s second destruction. It was destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar at the beginning of his reign, when the entire city was demolished and left desolate forever. Concerning this it is written, “The book of the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite.” “Woe to the city of blood,” which sheds blood. “It is entirely falsehood”—all its inhabitants denied Hashem and His existence. “It is full of plunder.” Although it is filled with the flesh of its victims, nevertheless, “prey never departs”—its inhabitants continually seize new victims, murdering and destroying lives.

“The sound.” First, he depicts the city’s constant tumult: “the sound of the whip and the rattling sound of wheels” are continually heard. Second, he depicts the danger that pervades the city, where there is always “a galloping horse and a bounding chariot.”

“The horseman charges.” On the ascent to the mountains, where chariots and horses cannot go, the horseman is found, together with “the flashing sword and the gleaming spear,” for the warriors take their stand there. Consequently, there is “a multitude of slain,” as people are killed in the streets, and “a mass of corpses.” They sweep the corpses away with brooms, as refuse is swept away. Nevertheless, “there is no end to the dead bodies,” for it is impossible to remove them all, until “they stumble over their corpses” as passersby trip over them.

“Because of the multitude.” The reason that such a vast multitude gathers there is “the multitude of the harlot’s prostitutions.” She is “gracefully alluring” and also “a mistress of sorceries,” ensnaring souls through witchcraft, until she “sells nations through her prostitutions.” Even distinguished families, which would not be seduced by prostitution, she sells “through her sorceries,” for sorcery operates beyond the natural order and can exert power even over eminent families. In the allegory, the nations are enticed to gather there by her great wealth and commerce, which are compared to a harlot’s wages, as explained in Isaiah 23. The distinguished families are enticed through her sorceries and schemes, by which she blinds their eyes and brings them into subjugation to her.

“Behold, I am against you, and I will uncover your skirts.” I will lift the filthy hems of your garments over your face. “I will show the nations” that were seduced by your prostitution “your nakedness,” and I will show the kingdoms that were seduced by your sorcery “your disgrace.”
“And I will cast abominations upon you” to disfigure your beauty, until “I make you contemptible” and an object of filth.

“And it shall be.” Thus, “everyone who sees you will flee” and distance himself “from you,” saying, “Nineveh has been devastated!” Since Nineveh had continually devastated the entire world, “who will mourn for her?” For everyone hates her. The prophet now turns toward Nineveh and addresses her: “From where shall I seek comforters for you?” To whom has such a calamity ever happened, so that I might comfort you by saying that the same thing also happened to someone else?

“Are you better?” He answers: I can indeed comfort you by saying, “Are you better than No-amon?” For it too was destroyed as you will be, and in its greatness it resembled you. No-amon was also a great and populous city. Just as you dwell upon the Tigris River, so “it dwelt among the rivers,” until “water surrounded it” on every side. Moreover, the sea encircled it, serving as its rampart and wall. Therefore, he says, “whose rampart was the sea,” and “whose wall was from the sea.” Both its great outer wall and its smaller inner fortification were formed by the sea.

“Cush.” She also possessed greater strength and more military assistance than you, for “Cush was her strength,” and “Egypt” herself supplied forces “without end,” since her people were exceedingly numerous. Moreover, “Put and the Libyans, who were among your allies” and assisted Nineveh, were likewise among Egypt’s allies at that time.

“She too went into exile,” just as you will. “Her infants too were dashed to pieces,” as happened to you, “and they cast lots for her nobles” to determine by lot who would take each of them as slaves.

“You too.” That is, I will comfort you by telling you that the same fate befell—or will befall—a great city like yourself. The prophet depicts you as drinking a cup of consolation, as mourners customarily do when receiving comfort, and becoming intoxicated from that cup. Through this, “you will become hidden,” disappearing from sight as though you no longer existed in the world. “You too will become intoxicated”—you who now “seek a stronghold against the enemy” and expect to take refuge in a fortress and escape. This will not help you, for—

“All your fortresses are like fig trees bearing first-ripe figs.” With the slightest movement, “if they are shaken, they fall” from the tree directly “into the mouth of the eater.” First-ripe figs fall more easily than figs that have not yet ripened. Likewise, the fortresses that will now be the first to mature for conquest will be captured with exceptional ease.
“Behold.” There is no one capable of fighting in defense of the fortresses, for “your people are like women,” who are not warriors. Therefore, “the gates of your land have been thrown wide open.”

“The waters of the siege.” The prophet mocks their efforts to strengthen their fortresses and seek protection within them. One who wishes to shut himself inside a city under siege must have abundant reservoirs of water prepared for him. You, however, have no ready supply of water; rather, “draw for yourself water for the siege”—water drawn into vessels, which is limited in quantity and will not last many days because it will become foul. “Strengthen your fortresses,” for they are not strong. He then says mockingly, “Enter the mud and tread the clay.” Mud is unsuitable for making bricks, which are made from clay rather than mud trampled beneath human feet; bricks made of mud will crumble and turn to dust. But since you have no clay from which to make bricks, enter the mud and tread it as though trampling the mud could make it as firm as clay. Therefore, I tell you, “Grasp the brick mold firmly.” You will have to hold the mold very securely so that the brick does not crumble into fragments, for in truth it is made of mud.

“There.” But there, while you are treading the mud to strengthen your fortresses, the enemy’s fire will consume you; the sword will cut you off and devour you like the young locust that consumes the grass of the field. “Multiply yourself like the young locust.” The young locust is one of the species of locust. When it first emerges, it is a larva; after a time, it encloses itself within a covering, as most creeping creatures enclose themselves in a sheath. It remains there for a fixed period and then emerges from the covering as a winged creature, becoming a kind of locust and flying away. Accordingly, the prophet compares the multitude of merchants and peoples found in Nineveh to the young locust while it is still a larva, crawling upon the ground and unable to fly. But after Nineveh is conquered, they will emerge from their coverings, grow wings, and become like locusts that fly away from the land. Thus, you seek to make yourself numerous like the young locust through the merchants who crawl throughout your city like creeping locusts; but you will become numerous like the winged locust, for they will soon grow wings and fly away from the land.

“You multiplied.” He explains the meaning of “Multiply yourself like the young locust.” For “you multiplied your peddlers”—the small merchants who sell their goods to individual customers—“beyond the stars of heaven.” They were within you like young locusts crawling from place to place but never leaving the territory in which they lived. Now, however, you will become like the winged locust, for “the young locust sheds its skin”—it casts off its covering, emerges from its enclosure as a winged locust, “and flies away” to another land. That is, they have now all abandoned you.

“Your crowned officials.” The governors and deputies whom you adorned with diadems and crowns likewise resembled winged locusts. Just as locusts fly elsewhere, they rebelled against you and flew away to seek refuge under the protection of Nebuchadnezzar, your conqueror. “Your military commanders”—those appointed over the army—resembled “swarms of locusts,” gatherings of various kinds of locusts whose habit is “to camp within the walls on a cold day.” There they remain hidden and dormant throughout the winter. But when “the sun rises,” then “each flies away” on its own, “and no one knows where it has gone.” Likewise, throughout the war, these commanders hid within the walls and holes, as though asleep, and did nothing. When the city gates were opened, each fled for his own life.

“They slumbered.” He explains that “your shepherds slumbered”—the leaders whom you appointed over the army slept. Consequently, “your mighty men remained at rest”: your warriors stayed in their dwellings and did not go out to fight. Likewise, “your people rested”—the entire army ceased its activity and did not fight. Now “they are scattered upon the mountains, with no one to gather them.” This is the meaning of the image, “When the sun rises, each flies away”: they have dispersed over the mountains, and no one gathers them together.

“There is no grieving spirit for your ruin.” That is, no one will be found whose spirit grows faint over you or who grieves for your destruction. “There is no suffering spirit for your wound.” Even over the wound that follows the ruin, no one is pained or distressed for you. On the contrary, “everyone who hears the report of you”—the report of your destruction—“claps his hands over you” as a sign of rejoicing, “for upon whom has your wickedness not continually passed?” You inflicted evil upon many peoples, and therefore they all rejoice over your downfall.
